screens.title: Building Responsive UIs with Layout Widgets & Media Queries
screens.subtitle: Make layouts adapt to screen size, orientation, and available space using Flutter's core widgets.

narration.text: Responsive UI means an app that reliably looks and works well across many device sizes and orientations. In this chapter you'll learn a small toolbox: MediaQuery for global device metrics, LayoutBuilder for local parent constraints, Flexible and Expanded for distributing space inside Rows and Columns, and OrientationBuilder for orientation-specific layouts. These tools form a progression: use MediaQuery for big breakpoints, LayoutBuilder for components that must adapt to their container, Flexible and Expanded to size children proportionally, and OrientationBuilder when you want a completely different layout in portrait versus landscape. I'll show concrete code examples and a hands-on product card activity that switches between stacked and side-by-side layouts based on available width. A common beginner mistake is using the wrong level of responsiveness — for example, reading the full screen width inside a small composited card instead of its parent's constraints. We'll contrast that with correct use of LayoutBuilder. By the end you'll be able to design components that adapt gracefully and avoid awkward stretching or wasted space. Notice the three topic cards here that preview MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder, and Flex widgets — they will guide our hands-on practice and checks for responsiveness.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Pick the right tool for the scale of adaptation: MediaQuery for global breakpoints, LayoutBuilder for local constraints, Flexible/Expanded for proportional layout, and OrientationBuilder for orientation switches.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will build a practical skillset for making UIs that adapt. First, you'll understand responsive design principles in Flutter: what responsiveness means, why parent constraints matter, and how to match layout strategies to the problem. Second, you'll use MediaQuery to read device properties such as width, height, pixel density and orientation, which lets you make global breakpoint choices like switching from one to two columns. Third, you'll learn to use LayoutBuilder to read the space a parent actually gives a component, enabling self-contained widgets that adapt whether they're full-screen or nested. Fourth, you'll master Flexible and Expanded so you can distribute space inside Rows and Columns without awkward stretching. Each objective connects a concrete coding skill to a reason it matters: maintainable layouts, fewer visual bugs across devices, and components that are reusable. A short in-chapter activity asks you to implement a product card that stacks or rows itself at a 600 pixel threshold, reinforcing the right tool for the right level of adaptation. This learning path reduces guesswork and helps you write layouts that behave predictably on phones and tablets.

screens.title: Bloom: Learn → Understand → Apply → Master
screens.subtitle: How these objectives map to practice and verification

narration.text: This second objectives slide maps the skills to practical actions. Learning begins with being able to name the widgets and describe their roles: MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder, Flexible, Expanded, and OrientationBuilder. Understanding means you can choose when to use a global metric versus local constraints and explain why Expanded forces tight-fitting behavior while Flexible allows loose fitting. Applying requires you to implement a responsive product card or to refactor an existing screen so it uses LayoutBuilder where nested sizing matters. Mastery means extracting adaptive components that are reusable and performant, and reducing unnecessary rebuilds by moving stable parts out of frequently rebuilt builders. A useful misconception to check: do not reach for MediaQuery inside every nested widget; instead prefer LayoutBuilder when adapting a component to its parent's space. The competency milestones in each objective pair a code task with a verification: run the app at multiple sizes or use emulators to confirm layout changes. Practicing this progression helps you avoid over- or under-reacting to available space and keeps your UI both flexible and predictable.

keyIdea.title: Skill progression

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Bloom Progression
Learn & Understand

  • Understand fit behavior: Expanded is tight, Flexible can be loose and respects intrinsic size.
  • Contrast common mistakes: reading full-screen metrics in nested widgets causes brittle layouts.
Apply & Master

  • Master by extracting components and minimizing rebuilds triggered by LayoutBuilder or OrientationBuilder.

Quick mnemonic
Think "global vs local": MediaQuery = global, LayoutBuilder = local, Flexible/Expanded = inside-row sizing.

screens.title: What is Responsive UI in Flutter?
screens.subtitle: Definition, why it matters, and a simple example scenario

narration.text: Responsive UI in Flutter means designing interfaces that adapt their layout and sizing to different screens and orientations so the app remains usable and visually coherent. A responsive design addresses three conditions: the global device metrics like screen width and orientation; the local constraints a parent widget gives a child; and the distribution of leftover space among siblings. For example, a product listing might show a single column of cards on a phone and two columns on a tablet — this uses a global breakpoint decision. Another example is a card inside a grid: the card should adapt to the cell's size, which is a local constraint problem. If a component ignores its parent's constraints and always assumes full screen, it will overflow or look sparse when nested. A common misconception is treating responsiveness as only changing font sizes; it's primarily about structure, spacing, and how widgets share available space. In practice you combine small, reusable components that each adapt to their given size, then compose them into screens that respond at the global level. To check your understanding, imagine the same app on a small phone, a large phone, and a tablet — list which widgets should be responsive globally and which should be responsive locally.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Responsive UI adapts structure and sizing across devices by combining global metrics, local constraints, and proportional space distribution.

content.html:
Core Concept What is Responsive UI?
Definition & rationale
Responsive UI combines global breakpoints, local constraints, and proportional sizing to make apps usable on many devices. It reduces overflow, wasted space, and visual inconsistencies.
Concrete scenario
A product list shows one column on phones and two columns on tablets using a global width check. A card inside that list adapts to its grid cell using local constraints.
Common mistake
Using full-screen MediaQuery values inside a nested widget causes brittle layouts that don't respect parent sizes.
Key Takeaway

Design components to adapt to their own constraints, and use global checks only for top-level breakpoints.

Quick checklist for responsive design
  • Identify which elements need global breakpoints (lists, major layout changes).
  • Identify which elements must adapt to parent space (cards, buttons, mini-widgets).
  • Decide where to use Flexible or Expanded to distribute leftover space in rows or columns.
  • Test on multiple widths and orientations to catch edge cases.

screens.title: MediaQuery: Reading global device metrics
screens.subtitle: How to use MediaQuery.of(context) and common use cases

narration.text: MediaQuery exposes global information about the device and environment: screen size, orientation, pixel density, and text scale. You access it using MediaQuery. of(context). size. width or. height for direct numbers. Use these values for top-level decisions like switching between one and two columns, increasing horizontal padding on larger screens, or choosing different image sizes. A practical use is conditional rendering: if the width is below a threshold, render a single-column list; above that threshold, switch to a grid. However, be careful—MediaQuery returns the full screen metrics, not the space a particular parent gives a nested widget. That is why we reserve MediaQuery for page-level or global breakpoints. A common example: when showing articles, use MediaQuery to decide whether to use a ListView or a GridView with two columns. To test, run your app on different emulators and manually change window sizes where possible. Remember also to consider text scale factor from MediaQuery for accessibility adjustments. As a quick misconception check: if a small card inside a larger screen needs to adapt, prefer LayoutBuilder rather than MediaQuery. MediaQuery: Reading global device metrics means use mediaquery for global, top-level breakpoint decisions. avoid using it to size deeply nested widgets.. In practical terms, how to use mediaquery.of(context) and common use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: MediaQuery tip
keyIdea.text: Use MediaQuery for global, top-level breakpoint decisions. Avoid using it to size deeply nested widgets.

content.html:
Definition MediaQuery
MediaQuery usage
Access global screen metrics for top-level layout decisions and accessibility adjustments.
// Example: check width and switch layout
final width = MediaQuery.of(context).size.width;
if (width < 600) {
  // show single-column ListView
} else {
  // show GridView with 2 columns
}
Practical uses
  • Global breakpoints for lists vs grids.
  • Choosing larger image assets on tablets.
  • Respecting textScaleFactor for accessibility.
Concrete example
Use MediaQuery.of(context).size.width to choose between a ListView and GridView for article layouts at a 768 pixel threshold.
Misconception
Don't use MediaQuery inside a small card that needs to adapt to its parent. That causes mismatch between component size and decision logic.
Key Takeaway

MediaQuery is ideal for page-level breakpoints and accessibility settings; use it thoughtfully.

screens.title: LayoutBuilder: Adapting to parent constraints
screens.subtitle: Use parent constraints to make modular, self-contained components

narration.text: LayoutBuilder gives a builder function with BoxConstraints for the parent space, telling a widget how much room it may occupy. This is different from MediaQuery: LayoutBuilder is local and reactive to the immediate parent, so it's perfect for cards, buttons, or any component that may appear in different container sizes. A common pattern is checking constraints. maxWidth and switching between a Column and a Row layout. For example, inside a card you might render image above text when maxWidth is under 600, and side-by-side when it's wider. LayoutBuilder rebuilds its child whenever the parent's constraints change, so place only adaptive parts inside it to avoid unnecessary rebuilds of the whole screen. Another practical tip: extract stable widgets out of the builder closure so they don't rebuild on every constraint change. Misusing LayoutBuilder by embedding heavy widget trees directly in the builder can cause performance issues. To verify behavior, simulate parent size changes with a SizedBox or by resizing a browser window in debug mode. Finally, use LayoutBuilder to make components self-sufficient: they decide their own layout based on the space they actually have.

keyIdea.title: LayoutBuilder advantage
keyIdea.text: LayoutBuilder reacts to the space a parent provides, enabling modular components that adapt whether full-screen or nested.

content.html:
Process Flow LayoutBuilder
How to decide inside LayoutBuilder
Check constraints.maxWidth and choose structure: stack vertically on narrow widths, arrange horizontally on wider widths.
LayoutBuilder(
  builder: (context, constraints) {
    if (constraints.maxWidth < 600) {
      return Column(children: [Image(), TextBlock()]);
    } else {
      return Row(children: [Image(), Expanded(child: TextBlock())]);
    }
  },
)
  • Use LayoutBuilder for components that may be nested or resized by parents.
  • Extract non-adaptive children out of the builder to reduce rebuild cost.
  • Prefer constraints checks for layout-switching, not global width values inside nested widgets.
Example
A ProductCard uses LayoutBuilder to choose Column when its parent cell is narrow, and Row with Expanded text when wide.
Pro tip
Test by wrapping the component in different SizedBox widths to simulate parent constraint changes during development.
Key Takeaway

Use LayoutBuilder to make components that responsibly adapt to the space they receive, keeping layout logic local.

screens.title: Flexible vs Expanded
screens.subtitle: Understand the difference between loose and tight fitting in Flex layouts

narration.text: Flexible and Expanded are tools for distributing leftover space along a Row or Column's main axis. Expanded is a specialized Flexible with fit set to tight, so it forces its child to fill the available space; multiple Expanded widgets share leftover space according to their flex values. Flexible with the default loose fit allows the child to be up to the available space but doesn't require it to stretch beyond its intrinsic size. Practically, use Expanded when you want a text field in a chat input to occupy the remaining width and push other elements to the sides. Use Flexible when the child should grow if space exists but stay at its intrinsic size otherwise, such as a button that should not be stretched to fill too much width. Common mistakes include using Expanded for every child which can lead to unnaturally stretched widgets. A concrete example: in a Row with two fixed buttons and a central text input, wrapping the text input in Expanded makes it take all remaining width. If you wrapped both a button and input in Expanded they will split remaining space, which might not be desirable. Test with multiple flex values to allocate proportional space.

keyIdea.title: Flex tip
keyIdea.text: Expanded forces tight filling of remaining space; Flexible with loose fit lets children remain at intrinsic size while expanding if room exists.

content.html:
Comparison Flexible vs Expanded
How they behave
Expanded = Flexible(fit: FlexFit.tight). Flexible default = FlexFit.loose. Use Expanded to force children to fill; Flexible to allow optional growth.
Row(
  children: [
    Expanded(
      child: TextField(),
    ),
    SizedBox(width: 8),
    Flexible(
      child: ElevatedButton(child: Text('Send')),
    ),
  ],
)
  • Expanded divides leftover space by flex values.
  • Flexible lets a child stay at its intrinsic size if it prefers.
  • Choose based on whether you want forced distribution or optional growth.
Concrete example
A chat input: TextField wrapped with Expanded fills remaining width; a small Send button wrapped with Flexible keeps its size but can grow if needed.
Common mistake
Wrapping every child in Expanded causes uniform splitting that often makes controls look stretched and unusable.
Key Takeaway

Use Expanded for forced distribution and Flexible for optional growth to preserve intrinsic sizing where appropriate.

screens.title: Chat input example with Expanded & Flexible
screens.subtitle: Walk through a practical Row example and expected sizing behavior

narration.text: Let's walk through a concrete code example that shows Expanded and Flexible in action. Imagine a Row with a text input, a small gap, and a send button. Wrapping the text input in Expanded makes it take all leftover horizontal space. The send button wrapped in Flexible will size itself according to its intrinsic width and only grow if the remaining space forces it. This is the typical chat input arrangement where the message field should use as much room as possible and buttons remain compact. Common misinterpretations include assuming Flexible will always shrink a child; Flexible with loose fit gives the child a chance to keep its natural width and only expand when space allows. For debugging, inspect layout bounds and test with different device widths or by resizing the emulator window. If two widgets should split space proportionally, wrap both in Expanded and set flex values to control the proportion. For performance, avoid placing large trees inside the builder that rebuilds often. The main takeaway is to match the child's intended sizing behavior to Flexible or Expanded so the interface feels natural across device widths.

keyIdea.title: Practical example
keyIdea.text: A Row with Expanded text input and Flexible send button gives a predictable chat input that scales well across widths.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough Expanded & Flexible in a Row
Example code
Row(
  children: [
    Expanded(
      child: TextField(
        decoration: InputDecoration(hintText: 'Type your message...'),
      ),
    ),
    SizedBox(width: 8),
    Flexible(
      child: ElevatedButton(onPressed: () {}, child: Text('Send')),
    ),
  ],
)
  • Expanded forces the TextField to claim remaining width.
  • Flexible allows the button to remain its natural size unless more space is available.
  • Use SizedBox for predictable gaps instead of padding inside children.
Scenario
Chat input in portrait should keep the button compact and let the text field scale; on tablets the same code adapts naturally.
Check your understanding
What happens if you wrap both the text field and button with Expanded and give them flex 1? They will split remaining space evenly.
Key Takeaway

Choose Expanded for forced fill and Flexible for components that should keep intrinsic size when practical.

screens.title: OrientationBuilder: Layouts by orientation
screens.subtitle: Switch entire layouts when portrait or landscape changes

narration.text: OrientationBuilder is a widget that rebuilds its child whenever the device orientation changes between portrait and landscape. Use it when you want to provide completely different arrangements, not just minor sizing tweaks. For example, you might show a vertically scrolling list in portrait but a grid view in landscape to make better use of horizontal space. The builder gives you an orientation value to test and choose between two widget trees. Keep in mind OrientationBuilder listens for orientation changes at the device level, so use it for screen-level layout switches rather than per-card adjustments. A common misconception is to overuse OrientationBuilder for small widgets; prefer LayoutBuilder for local constraint-driven changes. When using OrientationBuilder, extract stable parts of the UI that do not depend on orientation into separate widgets to limit rebuild scope. Also combine OrientationBuilder with MediaQuery and LayoutBuilder: MediaQuery may guide global breakpoints, OrientationBuilder may swap whole screen arrangements, and LayoutBuilder adjusts components inside those arrangements. Finally, verify orientation-dependent UIs on both small and large devices to ensure the landscape layout is meaningful and usable. OrientationBuilder: Layouts by orientation means use orientationbuilder for layout-wide swaps between portrait and landscape; prefer layoutbuilder for local, container-level adjustments.. In practical terms, switch entire layouts when portrait or landscape changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Orientation tip
keyIdea.text: Use OrientationBuilder for layout-wide swaps between portrait and landscape; prefer LayoutBuilder for local, container-level adjustments.

content.html:
Core Concept OrientationBuilder
When to use orientation-aware layouts
Swap major widget arrangements to better leverage the screen's shape. Landscape often benefits from grids or side-by-side content.
OrientationBuilder(
  builder: (context, orientation) {
    if (orientation == Orientation.portrait) {
      return ListView(...);
    } else {
      return GridView.count(crossAxisCount: 4, ...);
    }
  },
)
  • Use for screen-level rearrangements, not micro-adjustments.
  • Combine with MediaQuery to tune breakpoints and with LayoutBuilder for nested adaptivity.
  • Keep stable UI parts outside the builder to limit rebuilds.
Concrete example
Show ListView in portrait and a dense GridView in landscape to present more items when there's extra width.
Performance note
Limit expensive rebuilds by moving non-orientation-dependent widgets out of the OrientationBuilder scope.
Key Takeaway

OrientationBuilder is ideal for swapping whole layouts between portrait and landscape to enhance usability.

screens.title: Combining the tools: a progressive approach
screens.subtitle: How to layer MediaQuery, LayoutBuilder and Flex widgets together

narration.text: A pragmatic approach is to build progressively. Start with a simple single-column layout. Add MediaQuery checks for page-level breakpoints that should change structure, such as switching from a ListView to a GridView when width passes a threshold. Inside those structures, use LayoutBuilder for components that must adapt to their parent cells. Finally, inside rows and columns, apply Flexible and Expanded to distribute leftover space predictably. This layered strategy reduces complexity and prevents conflicting logic: MediaQuery handles global stage direction, LayoutBuilder handles component-level decisions, and Flexible/Expanded fine-tune sibling sizing. A practical example: implement the product list page. Use MediaQuery to decide grid column count. Each product cell contains a ProductCard that uses LayoutBuilder to pick vertical stacking or side-by-side layout. Inside the ProductCard's Row, use Expanded for the description area and Flexible for action buttons. This pattern keeps responsibilities clear, simplifies debugging, and makes components reusable. A misconception is trying to solve all adaptivity from a single widget; layering keeps behavior modular and testable. As you refactor, extract adaptive parts into their own widgets to limit rebuilds and improve readability. Combining the tools: a progressive approach means layer global, local, and sibling-sizing tools: mediaquery for pages, layoutbuilder for components, flexible/expanded for sibling sizing.. In practical terms, how to layer mediaquery, layoutbuilder and flex widgets together. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Progressive layering
keyIdea.text: Layer global, local, and sibling-sizing tools: MediaQuery for pages, LayoutBuilder for components, Flexible/Expanded for sibling sizing.

content.html:
Process Flow Progressive approach
Layering strategy
MediaQuery for global breakpoints, LayoutBuilder for component constraint checks, Flexible/Expanded for internal space distribution.
Example flow
1) MediaQuery decides columns. 2) ProductCard uses LayoutBuilder to choose Column or Row. 3) Inside Row, Expanded is used for text and Flexible for buttons.
Why it matters
This separation reduces layout bugs and keeps each widget responsible for its own adaptivity.
Developer checklist
  • Choose MediaQuery for page-level changes.
  • Use LayoutBuilder for components used in different parent sizes.
  • Wrap inline flexible areas with Flexible or Expanded as needed.
Key Takeaway

Layer your responsiveness to keep logic local, predictable, and efficient.

screens.title: Adaptive Product Card activity
screens.subtitle: Implement a card that stacks under 600px and shows side-by-side at 600px or wider

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to implement a ProductCard that adapts based on available width. The requirement: if the width is less than 600 pixels, display the image above the text using a Column; if it's 600 pixels or more, display image and text side-by-side using a Row and wrap the text in Expanded. Use LayoutBuilder inside the ProductCard so it responds to its parent constraints rather than full-screen width. The starter code provides a Card with placeholder content; replace the static Column with a LayoutBuilder builder that checks constraints. maxWidth and returns the appropriate structure. This reinforces two lessons: choose LayoutBuilder for component-level adaptivity, and use Expanded to allow text to occupy remaining width in the Row layout. Test by wrapping the ProductCard in a SizedBox with different widths to simulate narrow and wide parents. A common pitfall is using MediaQuery inside the ProductCard; that will base decisions on full screen size rather than the parent container. After implementing, verify spacing, image sizing, and readable text across both modes. Adaptive Product Card activity means use layoutbuilder to create a productcard that switches between column and row at a 600px constraint boundary.. In practical terms, implement a card that stacks under 600px and shows side-by-side at 600px or wider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Use LayoutBuilder to create a ProductCard that switches between Column and Row at a 600px constraint boundary.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity Adaptive Product Card
Task
Replace the placeholder Column with a LayoutBuilder that checks constraints.maxWidth and returns Column for < 600 or Row with Expanded text for ≥ 600.
Starter hints
  • Keep image sizing reasonable in both modes.
  • Wrap the text area with Expanded when using Row.
  • Test with different SizedBox widths during development.
// Inside ProductCard.build
return LayoutBuilder(
  builder: (context, constraints) {
    if (constraints.maxWidth < 600) {
      return Column(children: [ImagePlaceholder(), TextBlock()]);
    } else {
      return Row(children: [ImagePlaceholder(), Expanded(child: TextBlock())]);
    }
  },
);
Testing tip
Wrap ProductCard in SizedBox(width: 500) and SizedBox(width: 700) to confirm both layouts.
Check
Does the card respond to parent width changes? If yes, you used LayoutBuilder correctly.

screens.title: Avoiding rebuild pitfalls and optimizing performance
screens.subtitle: Best practices when using builders and adaptive widgets

narration.text: While LayoutBuilder and OrientationBuilder rebuild on constraint or orientation changes, excessive or poorly scoped rebuilds can affect frame rate. To optimize, extract stable parts of your UI outside builders so they don't rebuild on every layout change. For example, if only the content arrangement changes but the header is static, move the header into a parent widget. Avoid placing large widget trees inside the builder closure. Another performance tip is to use const constructors where possible, so unchanged widgets are not rebuilt unnecessarily. Limit expensive computations inside builders; compute values once and pass them down. When debugging performance, profile frame rendering and check which widgets rebuild frequently. Also avoid nesting multiple builders when one will suffice; for example, prefer a single LayoutBuilder at the component boundary rather than several nested builders. Finally, remember that Flutter's rebuilds are fast, but layout and paint work can still add overhead. Emphasize clarity and separation of concerns: keep adaptive logic close to where it matters and extract reusable, stable widgets for better maintainability and performance. Avoiding rebuild pitfalls and optimizing performance means keep builders scoped tightly and extract stable widgets to minimize unnecessary rebuilds and layout work.. In practical terms, best practices when using builders and adaptive widgets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Performance
keyIdea.text: Keep builders scoped tightly and extract stable widgets to minimize unnecessary rebuilds and layout work.

content.html:
Performance & Best Practices
Reduce unnecessary rebuilds
Extract static parts out of builders, prefer const where possible, and limit heavy computations inside LayoutBuilder or OrientationBuilder closures.
  • Move headers and footers outside adaptive builders.
  • Use const constructors for unchanged widgets.
  • Avoid deep nested builders unless needed for separate adaptive concerns.
Quick checklist
  1. Scope builders narrowly.
  2. Extract stable children.
  3. Profile when in doubt.
Common pitfall
Embedding large trees in builders leads to frequent and expensive rebuilds that cost layout and paint time.
Key Takeaway

Keep adaptive logic local and efficient; extract stable UI to reduce rebuild scope and improve performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from the chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize three core concepts to remember. First, responsive UI is about choosing the right level for decisions: MediaQuery for global breakpoints and LayoutBuilder for component-level adaptivity. Second, Flexible and Expanded control how children share or claim leftover space inside Rows and Columns; Expanded enforces tight filling while Flexible allows loose growth. Third, OrientationBuilder is the tool for swapping entire layouts between portrait and landscape. Keep these ideas in mind as mental shortcuts when designing or refactoring layouts. Also, always test on multiple device sizes and orientations to find edge cases. These three concepts give you practical rules to guide layout choices and to prevent common errors like using global metrics inside nested widgets. What to Remember
MediaQuery
Global device metrics for page-level breakpoints and accessibility settings.
LayoutBuilder
Use parent constraints to adapt component structure where it matters most.
Flexible & Expanded

Takeaway

Use global metrics for stage direction, local constraints for components, and flex widgets for sibling sizing. Test on devices and minimize builder scope for performance.

narration.text: Three final reminders: First, prefer LayoutBuilder inside components that might be nested so decisions are based on actual available space. Second, avoid overusing MediaQuery for nested decisions — it should guide page-level choices. Third, keep adaptive logic focused and extract constant widgets out of builders to reduce rebuild work and maintain smooth animations. Practically, when you implement the product card activity, check that it responds to parent width changes by altering structure and that its internal spacing looks natural. These habits make your UI resilient and reusable. As a closing thought, responsiveness is not only about fitting content; it's about making layouts predictable and comfortable for users across devices. Ask yourself as you design: which widget should decide the layout here — the page, the parent component, or the sibling group?

keyIdea.title: Final thought
keyIdea.text: Responsiveness is a design discipline: pick the right decision scope, extract stable parts, and test widely to build predictable UIs.
